en: The Sūtra on the Ten Powers of the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Enfeoffed as Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, who was conferred the Purple Robe.
Translated by the Śramaṇa臣 (Chen) Shihu and others, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses ten powers. One who is endowed with these powers is able to thoroughly understand the vast and supreme states, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel."
What are these ten? They are as follows:
the Tathāgata knows all that is possible (*sthāna*) as it truly is, and he also knows all that is impossible (*asthāna*) as it truly is.
Because he knows this through direct realization, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s first power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with this power, is able to fully comprehend the vast and supreme bases of mastery, to roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and to turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, all actions performed by sentient beings in the past, future, and present—including their objects, locations, causes, and results."
Because of knowing this as it truly is, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s second power of knowledge regarding karma.

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with this power, he is able to fully comprehend the vast and supreme spheres of influence; he utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, all the states of meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti, whether defiled or purified, as well as the various factors of these concentrations."
Because he knows this through direct realization, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s third power of knowledge regarding meditative concentration.

Possessing this power, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to fully comprehend the vast and sublime states, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the wondrous Brahma-wheel.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various faculties of all sentient beings, whether themselves or others.
Because he knows them as they truly are, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s fourth power of knowledge regarding the faculties."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with this power, is able to fully comprehend the vast and supreme bases of mastery, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings.
Because he knows them as they truly are, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s fifth power of knowledge regarding inclinations and understandings."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with this power, is able to fully comprehend the vast and supreme states, roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various elements and the nature of infinite elements.
Because he knows them as they truly are, this is the Tathāgata’s sixth power of knowledge regarding the nature of elements."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with this power, is able to thoroughly understand the vast and supreme bases of mastery, roar the lion’s roar in the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, all paths leading to every destination.
Because he knows them as they truly are, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s seventh power of knowledge: the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with this power, is able to fully comprehend the vast and sublime bases of mastery; he utters the lion’s roar in the great assembly and turns the wondrous Brahma-wheel.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, namely: one birth, two births, three, four, five, or ten, twenty, up to a hundred, a thousand, and even countless hundreds of thousands of births; throughout countless hundreds of thousands of eons of formation, eons of destruction, and eons of both formation and destruction. He knows, exactly as they were, the circumstances, the conditions, the laws, and the locations of those places where he was born among various sentient beings—such as his name, his clan, his lineage, his food and drink, his experiences of pleasure and pain, and the limits of his lifespan’s duration. Having reached the end of that life, he was born in such-and-such a place; from there he passed away and was born here; from here he passed away and was born there. In this way, he recollects these various types of past abodes with complete accuracy."
By virtue of knowing this truly, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s eighth power of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with this power, he is able to understand vast and supreme states, roar the lion's roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.

"Furthermore, with the Tathāgata’s pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he perceives all sentient beings in the world as they are born and as they pass away—whether beautiful or ugly, noble or lowly, whether born in a happy realm or born in an unhappy realm—and he knows and sees them exactly as they are, according to their respective karmic actions."

If sentient beings perform unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind—slandering the noble ones, giving rise to various false views, and accumulating the causes and conditions of such actions of false view—then, through those causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the miserable realms and are born in the hells.

If sentient beings perform various virtuous deeds of body, speech, and mind, do not revile the noble ones, and give rise to right view—then, with the collection of such karmic factors of right view as the cause, by virtue of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the celestial realms.
All such matters as these he knows according to reality.
Because he knows them according to reality, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s ninth power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñānabala*).

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with this power, he is able to fully comprehend vast and supreme states; amidst the great assembly, he utters the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata has exhausted all taints; the taints do not increase within him. His mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated. Having realized such a Dharma through knowledge, he personally attains its fruit, knowing according to reality: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.'"
Because he knows this through direct realization, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s tenth power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with this power, he is able to understand the vast and supreme states, roar the lion's roar amidst the great assembly, and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ten Powers of a Buddha*.
